content:
I've had a grant funded to allow me to spend some time over the next year formalising results for applied dynamics. Specifically Lyapunov stability theorems and converse theorems (the conditions under which Lyapunov functions exist) and similar results using auxiliary functions to bound time averages. The ultimate aim is to formalise some concrete certificates that show that particular nonlinear systems are globally stable, bounded, that kind of thing.

A first obvious step is to build some definitions of dynamical stability into mathlib. Currently mathlib's Dynamics is a bit inconsistent. Flows are defined but not used much. Fixed points and periodic points are defined only for discrete-time dynamical systems, not flows. On the other hand, OmegaLimits are defined very generally.

I would propose Dynamics/Stability.Lean, or maybe Dynamics/Stability/Defs.lean, which would contain definitions of Lyapunov, asymptotic and maybe exponential stability for sets and fixed points. What I do not know is whether to do this for maps or flows.

I'm still relatively new to Mathlib and would appreciate any suggestions or advice.

Hi Jeremy, I am working on stability theory as well. I agree that the current state of dynamical systems is a bit lackluster. While it would certainly be possible to get basic notions of stability into mathlib, I am not sure that this a good idea. There are two problems: (a) the lack of maintainers with knowledge in control theory (b) proving theorems in the mathlib generality is harder for applied maths, because the literature is less concerned with abstraction (and might try to avoid it), so finding the right definitions might take a lot of trial and error.

We (Iman Shames and I) choose instead to have a library downstream of mathlib that is does the applied side and then upstream the mathematics that is missing in mathlib. We do have Lyapunov stability and LaSalle's invariance principle (the later can probably be generalized), but no exponential stability or converse theorems, that would be a very welcome contribution. Also having more real-world examples is something we would like to have. I haven't thought to deeply about a contribution policy, but I very much believe in open development and I would like to get other people involved in this project.
Link: https://github.com/mcdoll/DynamicalSystems

Hi @Moritz Doll , it's great to see that other people are thinking about this too and that project looks like an excellent start. I agree that eventually some things will have to be downstream of mathlib, but I'm not sure I completely follow your logic.

Part of my grant proposal was about building up momentum for other applied mathematicians to use formal verification and to break down the barriers that currently exist between, for example, applied dynamicists and ergodic theorists. To that end, I think as much as possible should be implemented in full generality in mathlib, and then concrete examples downstream to show how to use these in "the real world".

I think the most impact can be made by building these concepts into the massively successful existing library of mathlib. I don't think what I'm proposing is controversial, these are well-defined mathematical concepts.

Also, for the converse theorems, it could get quite deep in analysis, so that feels like mathlib is right place for it.

If the problem is that there aren't enough dynamicists in the mathlib community, well that's exactly what I'm trying to rectify, and I'm here to contribute!

I think part of the difference here is the timeline. I'm sure Moritz would also love to see more dynamical systems in mathlib (as would I, for that matter). The question is how to get there. Eventually, this should be in mathlib. I see at least two reasons why this is perhaps not the best short-term state.

Formalisation is an art (as Kevin Buzzard says): finding the right way to express a piece of mathematics in Lean can be non-trivial; there are design decisions to make (and often these can only be evaluated with experience). It's simply often unlikely you'll get a Lean definition right the first time, without testing it by formalising a useful application. For this reason, maintainers are generally sceptical of accepting a definition without evidence it's the right one. "I have built this library on it, and it has worked well in practice" is much better evidence.
Secondly, mathlib code needs to be maintained all the time: be that adapting to Lean changes, coherence with the rest of mathlib, etc. Accepting mathlib code is a commitment to maintaining it. Maintaining a contribution you don't understand is much more difficult: we would much prefer having in-house expertise if a proof breaks because of a change to Lean or a mathlib tactic.

We're in vigorous agreement about aiming for generality, or building momentum towards using formal verification in dynamics. (But I don't see why that cannot happen in DynamicalSystems to start. It might even be easier, as the barrier to contribution could be lower, allowing for faster iteration.)

Let me emphasize that having dynamics material is mathlib is an outcome probably everybody in this thread wants. But the short-term path may be via a separate project first.

Yes of course, I absolutely realise the need for agreement on the definitions, that's why I started this thread.

I'm happy to work in another project and then try to upstream things later but I guess the question is, if now is not the right time, then when? The stability definitions in DynamicalSystems look very reasonable to me and I don't see why we couldn't have that conversation in a pull request.

On the other hand, I'm a bit reluctant to work entirely in DynamicalSystems immediately because I don't understand the intentions or scope of this project, and it's not written to be compatible with the existing definitions in Mathlib's Flow.lean

@Michael Rothgang if your comment about maintenance of mathlib code was because I said I had a one year grant then please don't interpret that to mean I would abandon this after one year, I'm definitely sticking around, I just have some teaching buyout to focus on this.

If you have a Flow, then you can use the definition of stability, because a flow coerces to a function. This is done for a lot of the times in the repo.
About the scope: everything that concerns dynamical systems and stability is in scope. The goal is to build a library for formalized control theory, where ultimately some parts will live in mathlib and some parts will stay separate, but in a way that is invisible to someone using the library.
I don't think Michael's concern is a about you disappearing. Every line of code that mathlib accepts is to some extend a commitment that something upstream changes, this line of code will be changed. Also mathlib is now committed to tell downstream projects when a declaration changes names, where the new declaration is, which increases the amount of work if something gets refactored.
I think in the long run, I expect mathlib might switch to more a model where there are experimental repositories for different parts of maths and only once a chunk of code has matured enough it will get upstreamed to mathlib. The current model is totally hitting a wall with having 2.7k open PRs and the maintainers spending a lot of time removing AI slop and dealing with a lot of technical dept that has accumulated over time (and some coming from Lean being too lax in some of its checks).
